h1: The 5 Best Y Peelers of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 5 Y peelers scored on blade steel, handle grip, eye remover and care, from the OXO Good Grips to a serrated Piranha.
summary: The OXO Good Grips Y-Peeler is the one most kitchens should own: hardened stainless blade, soft handle, built-in potato eyer and dishwasher-safe care. The Kuhn Rikon Piranha earns a second drawer slot for tomatoes, peaches and kiwi, where a straight blade skids. The KitchenAid adds a lifetime limited warranty. Every peeler here costs under $25, so grip and blade type decide the ranking.
intro: A Y peeler lives or dies on one detail most reviews skip: how its blade pivots. A good one floats slightly in its frame, so the edge follows a potato's curve instead of digging into it. A rigid one gouges, and then you blame your knife skills. That is why two peelers with the same stainless steel can feel nothing alike in the hand.

We ranked five Y peelers on the Primea framework: blade steel and edge type, handle comfort and grip, extras like a potato eyer, and how each one is cleaned. All five are under $25, so the contest is about feel and care. Where the listings leave something out, we say so instead of guessing, and we scored on the specification sheet.

products.name: OXO Good Grips Y-Peeler
products.verdict: Hardened stainless blade, soft non-slip handle and a potato eyer. The default Y peeler.
products.description:
OXO's Y-Peeler uses a hardened stainless steel blade with a soft, non-slip handle, and carries a built-in potato eyer plus a removable blade cover. It is dishwasher safe, and priced in the under $25 bucket.

It ranks first because it has no real weakness. The handle is the softest in the group, which matters when you peel a bag of potatoes, and the blade cover protects both the edge and your fingers in a drawer. Against the KitchenAid it matches the dishwasher care, and where the KitchenAid offers a warranty, OXO offers the better grip. Its stainless edge will not have the bite of a carbon blade.

A safe buy for everyday vegetables. The caveat is that a plain straight blade slips on tomato skin.
cons: Stainless edge less keen than carbon
products.idealFor: Cooks who want one comfortable Y peeler for everyday vegetables.
products.skipIf: You regularly peel tomatoes, peaches or kiwi.

products.name: Kuhn Rikon Piranha Y Peeler
products.verdict: A serrated stainless blade that grips slick skins. The tomato and peach specialist.
products.description:
Kuhn Rikon's Piranha uses a serrated stainless steel blade on a 6.25 inch body with a non-slip handle. It suits either hand, and it is dishwasher safe in the under $25 bucket.

The serrations are the point. A smooth edge slides over a tomato or a ripe peach, while teeth bite the skin and let the blade travel. That specialist skill puts it second, just behind the OXO, which is the better general peeler for potatoes and carrots because a smooth edge gives thinner, more even strips. The Piranha makes sense as a second peeler, not a first.

Best for cooks who handle soft or slick skins often. The caveat is that serrated teeth can leave a slightly rougher finish on firm root vegetables.
products.idealFor: Cooks who peel tomatoes, peaches and other slick skins as often as potatoes.
products.skipIf: You want one peeler for potatoes and carrots only.

products.name: KitchenAid Y Peeler
products.verdict: A 420 stainless single-edge blade with a lifetime limited warranty. The long-term buy.
products.description:
KitchenAid pairs a 420 stainless single-edge blade with a glossy ABS handle trimmed in chrome at the bolster and endcap. It includes a plastic blade guard and a lifetime limited warranty, and it sits in the under $25 bucket.

The warranty is the differentiator, and it is why this ranks above the carbon and rubber-handled picks below. Where it loses to the OXO is the handle: glossy ABS is slicker with wet hands than a soft-touch grip, a real consideration when you are peeling a pile of wet potatoes. The blade is stainless, which means low maintenance and no rust worries.

Choose it if a warranty matters to you. The caveat is a handle that is more polished than grippy.
cons: Glossy handle is slippery when wet
products.idealFor: Buyers who want a dishwasher-safe stainless Y peeler backed by a warranty.
products.skipIf: You peel wet vegetables in volume and need a soft grip.

products.name: Spring Chef Y-Shaped Peeler
products.verdict: Soft rubber handle, eye remover and a hanging hole. A grippy stainless alternative to OXO.
products.description:
Spring Chef gives you food-grade stainless steel blades and a soft rubber non-slip handle with a built-in potato eye remover. There is a hanging hole in the handle, the peeler is dishwasher safe, and it sits in the under $25 bucket.

It reads as the closest rival to the OXO, with the same soft grip, the same eyer and the same cleaning. It ranks below the OXO because the OXO adds a removable blade cover and the Spring Chef does not mention one, so the blade is exposed in a crowded drawer. The hanging hole is a thoughtful extra that solves that, by getting the peeler out of the drawer entirely.

Pick it for a soft rubber grip on a budget. The caveat is limited detail on steel grade.
products.idealFor: Cooks who want a soft rubber grip and an eye remover in a stainless Y peeler.
products.skipIf: You want a protective blade cover for drawer storage.

products.name: Mercer Culinary Y Swiss Peeler
products.verdict: A sharp high-carbon blade that cuts wide citrus strips. Hand wash only.
products.description:
Mercer's Y Swiss Peeler pairs a high-carbon blade with a polypropylene handle. It works left or right handed, cuts wide citrus strips and is priced in the under $25 bucket.

Carbon steel takes a sharper edge than stainless, which is what makes it the pick for citrus zest for cocktails, where a wide, thin strip of peel is the aim. The price is care. It is hand wash only and needs drying fully, because carbon steel rusts if left wet, and that keeps it fifth behind the four dishwasher-safe peelers that make no such demand.

For home bartenders and cooks who value sharpness. The caveat is a plain polypropylene handle, which has less cushion than OXO or Spring Chef.
cons: Carbon steel can rust if damp
products.idealFor: Home bartenders and cooks who want wide citrus strips and a sharp carbon edge.
products.skipIf: You put everything in the dishwasher.

methodology.title: Blade steel and edge
methodology.description: Stainless, carbon and serrated edges each behave differently. We scored sharpness, rust resistance and suitability for different skins.

methodology.title: Handle grip
methodology.description: Soft rubber, glossy ABS and polypropylene differ in comfort when wet. We compared stated materials.

methodology.title: Extras
methodology.description: A potato eyer, blade cover or hanging hole adds daily convenience, so we credited each one.

methodology.title: Care and durability
methodology.description: Dishwasher safe versus hand wash only, plus warranties, decided close results.

methodology.title: Versatility
methodology.description: We checked how many produce types each peeler handles, from potatoes to tomatoes to citrus.

whatMatters.detail: Stainless steel resists rust and survives the dishwasher, while carbon steel takes a sharper edge but rusts if left damp. The OXO and KitchenAid use stainless, the Mercer uses high-carbon. Check the listing for the steel type and the care instructions, and pick carbon only if you will hand wash and dry the blade every single time, because even a short soak leaves rust spots.

A smooth edge glides over firm vegetables and gives thin, even strips. A serrated edge, like the Kuhn Rikon Piranha's, bites into slick skin that a smooth blade skids across. Think about what you peel most: potatoes and carrots favor smooth blades, while tomatoes, peaches and kiwi justify a serrated second peeler that lives in the same drawer.

A peeler is held for minutes at a time, often with wet hands. Soft rubber, as on the Spring Chef, and soft-touch grips such as the OXO resist slipping, while glossy ABS or hard polypropylene feel slicker. Read the handle material on the listing, and picture a wet, soapy hand holding it for a full bag of potatoes before you buy.

The small pointed tip beside the blade scoops out eyes and bruises, saving a separate knife. The OXO and Spring Chef include one, and the Piranha and Mercer do not list it. If you peel potatoes more than other produce, make the eyer a requirement, and look for it in the specs or photos, since it is a small pointed tip that is easy to miss.

A dishwasher-safe peeler saves a chore, and a warranty covers defects. The KitchenAid has a lifetime limited warranty, four of the five peelers are dishwasher safe, and the Mercer needs hand washing. Check the care line on the listing, and note whether any warranty applies to the specific product, because wording like lifetime limited usually covers defects, not wear.

howToChoose.intro: Start with the produce. Blade type matters more than brand.

cards.label: Stainless
cards.text: OXO, KitchenAid, Piranha and Spring Chef resist rust and handle the dishwasher, with a slightly softer edge.

cards.label: Carbon
cards.text: The Mercer takes a keener edge for citrus strips, but it needs hand washing and a full dry.

howToChoose.note: Default to stainless. Choose carbon only if you want the sharpest zest and will hand wash.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A symmetrical Y frame and a listing that states left or right handed use, since the blade must sit in line with either hand.

cards.label: In this ranking
cards.text: The Kuhn Rikon Piranha and Mercer both list left or right handed use.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You peel daily and want the warranty, which points to the KitchenAid.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You peel occasionally; the OXO or Spring Chef cost under $25 and last.

faq.q: Are Y peelers better than swivel peelers?
faq.a: For most cooks yes, because the Y frame lets you pull the blade toward you with a wide, steady stroke. The OXO and KitchenAid both use this shape. Swivel peelers can follow tight curves, but Y peelers handle bulk work with less wrist strain.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake?
faq.a: Using a smooth peeler on tomatoes, then pressing harder. That crushes the fruit. The Kuhn Rikon Piranha's serrated edge exists for this, so buy it as a second peeler instead of forcing the OXO.

faq.q: Is carbon steel worth it over stainless?
faq.a: Only for sharpness. The Mercer's high-carbon blade cuts wide citrus strips cleanly, but it needs hand washing and drying. The dishwasher-safe stainless OXO and KitchenAid suit most kitchens better, since their edges stay serviceable for years without any special care routine.
Peel away from your body on a stable surface, keep fingers behind the blade, and use the eyer on the OXO or Spring Chef for blemishes instead of cutting by hand. Replace a peeler that drags.

faq.q: How do I maintain the blade?
faq.a: Rinse stainless peelers such as the KitchenAid after use and dry them to avoid spots. Wash the Mercer by hand and dry fully. Replace any peeler whose blade no longer glides, since most are not designed for sharpening.

faq.q: Does a left-handed cook need a special peeler?
faq.a: Not with these. The Kuhn Rikon Piranha and Mercer both list left or right handed use, and a Y frame is symmetrical. Check the OXO's photos to see how the blade is oriented, then test with your dominant hand.

finalTake: The OXO Good Grips Y-Peeler is the right default: a hardened stainless blade, a soft handle and an eyer in a dishwasher-safe package. Add the Kuhn Rikon Piranha for tomatoes and peaches, take the KitchenAid for the lifetime limited warranty, and choose the Mercer only if you will hand wash a carbon blade for wide citrus strips.
